name: SQL and AI Training Data Pipelines
title: SQL and AI Training Data Pipelines
answer: Training and fine tuning data inside an organisation is usually assembled by pipelines that extract rows from operational databases, clean and join them with SQL, and load them where training jobs can read them, and mistakes in those queries become mistakes in the model. This scope covers feature tables, labels, text corpora, and evaluation sets that start life in relational systems. It also covers the return path, where model outputs and human feedback are written back into SQL tables for review and retraining. The focus is the data supply chain, not the model architecture itself.

sections.body: Training and fine tuning data inside an organisation is usually assembled by pipelines that extract rows from operational databases, clean and join them with SQL, and load them where training jobs can read them, and mistakes in those queries become mistakes in the model. This scope covers feature tables, labels, text corpora, and evaluation sets that start life in relational systems. It also covers the return path, where model outputs and human feedback are written back into SQL tables for review and retraining. The focus is the data supply chain, not the model architecture itself.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The pipeline runs on a mix of operational databases, analytical warehouses, object storage, and compute for training jobs. SQL engines such as PostgreSQL, MySQL, Snowflake, and BigQuery are common sources and staging layers, while orchestration tools like Airflow, dbt, and Spark move and transform data. This site itself is built from a PostgreSQL database, which shows how often the same relational systems serving applications become the first stop for training data. Access may be direct, through scheduled jobs, or through connectors that expose SQL to AI agents, and the site tracks 263 MCP servers for SQL databases and warehouses as one example of that connector layer.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work starts with SQL queries that select, filter, join, aggregate, and deduplicate source rows into a training set. Teams often materialise the result as a table or a file format such as Parquet, then split it into training, validation, and test sets. Labels may come from human annotation tables, business rules, or model outputs, and those labels are joined back to features with SQL. Because the query defines the training set, the SQL script and the source snapshot are part of the model's provenance. Version control, data tests, and row counts help catch silent changes before a training job reads the data.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in these pipelines turn on where the rows came from, what consent or licence covers them, and who can query them. SQL grants, row level security, masking, and retention rules are common controls at the database layer. Provenance is usually recorded by versioning the SQL, snapshotting source tables, and logging which query produced which training set. Risks include sensitive data leaking into a model, biased joins that skew labels, and stale or duplicated rows that quietly change behaviour. Organisations often add data catalogs, lineage graphs, and approval steps so that a training set can be traced back to its sources.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward more automation and more metadata. AI assistants are already drafting SQL for pipeline authors, with human review, and connectors that expose SQL to AI agents make that access easier. Pipelines are likely to become more declarative, with data contracts and tests expressed alongside the queries. Expect tighter links between SQL engines and training frameworks, so that a model can be retrained from a governed query rather than a hand copied export. Governance will keep moving left into the query layer, where access, lineage, and quality checks can be enforced before data reaches a training job.
